A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BoP/HedgeTune research, with matching authors and identifiable corresponding sections, equations, and experiments. Both main texts and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original toy simulations, synthetic reward-miscalibration experiments, and trained-proxy human-preference experiments, including four-seed results in Figures 9–12.

after.justification: V2 retains the original human-preference experiments and reports new HedgeTune evaluations on GPQA, MMLU Pro, and MATH using PPE responses.

M1.justification: V2 adds Soft Best-of-Poisson, combining a Poisson-distributed candidate count with softmax selection (Algorithm 5), and an optional discrete ternary search for BoN calibration (Appendix D). These extend the retained BoP sampler and HedgeTune residual-based optimization framework.

E1.justification: The synthetic TL;DR experiment using 60,000 summaries of one prompt is removed. V2 adds PPE-based evaluations on GPQA natural-science questions, MMLU Pro reasoning, and MATH problems. The mathematical toy example and AlpacaFarm human-preference coverage remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated alignment-method comparisons remain BoN, SBoN, and BoP, with tilted distributions retained in the toy example. The new reward models provide proxy scores rather than additional competing alignment methods. SBoP and the newly discussed mitigation methods are not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The new verifiable evaluations use binary correctness and expected accuracy, with candidate-count and temperature sweeps shown in Figures 3 and 5–8. These replace the synthetic study's calibrated probability of at least 10% reward improvement and its sampling grids. The retained human-preference training and evaluation settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: V1's controlled sensitivity to proxy-miscalibration thresholds and standalone toy temperature/tradeoff analysis are removed. V2 adds temperature-sensitivity analyses across candidate counts for four benchmark–reward-model pairs (Figures 5–8), examining how optimal hedging changes with sampling intensity. Human-preference noise and training-size analyses remain.

E5.justification: Removing the synthetic study also removes its explicit 300-bootstrap-replicate procedure and 95% confidence intervals. V2's new benchmark plots contain shaded bands without specifying their statistical interpretation or estimation procedure. The human-preference experiments retain the same four seeds.

E6.justification: V2 adds benchmark accuracy and temperature-sensitivity findings showing tuned SBoN sustaining accuracy after BoN declines, while removing the synthetic improvement results. The human-preference curves are retained. Separately, the reported matched-reward BoP KL-gap bound changes from 7 × 10^-3 to 8 × 10^-4.

T1.justification: V2 adds a discrete-policy hacking theorem, discrete BoN/BoP verification, and a general discrete BoP distribution and KL analysis (Appendices B.2 and C.2). It substantially replaces the near-optimality argument and adds SBoN log-partition, expected-reward, and KL claims in Appendix C.3. The central continuous-case hacking theorem remains.

C1.justification: The three central contributions—hacking characterization, BoP, and HedgeTune—remain. The abstract and introduction now explicitly claim empirical effectiveness on math, reasoning, and human-preference setups, and the introductory BoP approximation claim tightens from a KL gap of order 10^-3 to 10^-4.

C2.justification: V2 interprets larger optimal temperatures at larger candidate counts as stronger KL regularization. Appendix D.1 newly qualifies hedging as complementary to other mitigation methods and potentially offering only modest gains with weak proxies. The true-reward calibration requirement and SBoN numerical-instability caveat were already present.

D1.justification: V2 discloses Apple M3 CPU use and one A100 with 48 GPU-hours, replaces the anonymous code link with a named GitHub repository, and makes per-prompt calibration and solver details explicit. Conversely, it removes numerical quadrature, Monte Carlo sample-count, and parameter-grid details for the retained toy example.

R1.justification: New Appendix D.1 substantially expands the positioning against training-time regularization, reward-model improvements, regularized BoN, and inference-time pessimism, explaining operational tradeoffs. References also expand to cover PPE, the new benchmarks and proxy models, and additional pessimism and safety work. Numerous other reference edits merely update publication metadata.

P1.justification: The seven-section main narrative remains, with targeted revisions to the abstract, introduction, and uniform-reward explanation. V2 adds experimental subheadings, reorganizes appendix material into uniform and discrete cases, condenses repeated theorem presentations, and expands the conclusion.

P2.justification: V2 adopts the NeurIPS page and title layout, resizes and wraps Figure 2, replaces synthetic figures with benchmark plots, and adds four temperature-sweep grids. It removes the standalone toy tradeoff and summarization example figures and packs the retained human-preference appendix plots onto one page.

improvement.justification: V2 broadens empirical support with verifiable benchmarks and useful sensitivity analyses, while adding limitations and compute disclosures. However, new Appendix C.3 Equation (21) conflates conditional selection KL with marginal-policy KL: in the stated SBoN-to-BoN limit it yields log n, conflicting with the uniform-reference BoN value log n - 1 + 1/n given in v1 Appendix D.1. This new theoretical defect, alongside lost reproducibility details for the retained toy example, makes the net quality effect uncertain despite the empirical gains.
